title: Manaslu Circuit and Tsum Valley trek
meta_description: Manaslu Circuit and Tsum Valley trek, 20 nights: Mu Gompa and the Tsum nunneries, then Samagaon, the Larkya La (5,106 m) and Bhimthang.
summary: Twenty nights that join the Tsum Valley with the full Manaslu Circuit. You spend a week in Tsum, up to Mu Gompa at 3,700 m and back via Rachen nunnery, then follow the Budhi Gandaki into Nubri, rest at Samagaon and cross the Larkya La at 5,106 m to Bhimthang. Both permits, guide and porter included.
intro: If you have three weeks and want one walk that shows the Manaslu region fully, this is it. Tsum and Nubri sit side by side on the upper Budhi Gandaki, both Tibetan Buddhist, both close to the border, but each with its own dialect, gompas and customs. Doing Tsum first is also the best acclimatisation plan we know for the Larkya La: a week between 2,400 m and 3,700 m makes Samagaon, Samdo and the pass far kinder on your body.

The trip starts with a long drive to Machha Khola and three days up the gorge, then turns into Tsum at Lokpa. After Mu Gompa and the nunnery at Rachen, you come back down to the main valley, climb through Namrung and Lho to Samagaon, and cross the pass. Both Tsum and Manaslu are restricted areas: at least two trekkers, special permits and a licensed guide through a registered agency are required; check current status before you travel.
story: Three weeks is long enough for a valley to change you. The gorge comes first, hot and loud, then the narrow door into Tsum and a week among nunneries, mani walls and fields of barley where no animal is killed. You go up to Mu Gompa, a day from Tibet, and come down slower and quieter. Then Nubri: Ghap's carved stones, the first sight of Manaslu over Lho, yak herders in Samagaon, the old salt route at Samdo. By the time you cross the Larkya La at dawn, your legs and lungs are ready, and the long descent through Bhimthang's pines into the Marsyangdi feels earned. You finish on the Annapurna side, a whole mountain away from where you began.
highlights: Mu Gompa (3,700 m) and the nunneries of Rachen in Upper Tsum
Piren Phu, the cave associated with Milarepa, and the villages of Chhokangparo and Nile
Manaslu (8,163 m) over Lho and Samagaon
The Larkya La (5,106 m) with views of Himlung, Cheo Himal and Annapurna II
Natural acclimatisation in Tsum before the high pass

days.title: Arrive in Kathmandu, permit briefing
days.text: We meet you at Tribhuvan International Airport and settle you at Kathmandu Guest House in Thamel. Two restricted area permits, for Tsum and for Manaslu, are issued only through a registered agency with your original passport, so we handle the paperwork today or beforehand if you send your documents. Your guide comes to the hotel in the afternoon for a kit check and route briefing. With three weeks ahead, it is worth buying a spare pair of socks and a good map in Thamel.

days.title: Drive to Machha Khola
days.text: An early private jeep west along the Prithvi Highway, north from Dhading Besi on a rough road to Arughat, and up the Budhi Gandaki via Soti Khola to Machha Khola. It is a long and bumpy day, and a landslide can mean a short walk around a blocked section. Machha Khola is a small bazaar of lodges where trekkers for Manaslu and Tsum spend their first night. Eat well and sleep early; the walking starts tomorrow.

days.title: Up the gorge to Jagat
days.text: The trail follows the Budhi Gandaki upstream past Khorlabesi and the hot spring spouts of Tatopani, then over spurs and across suspension bridges to Dobhan. It climbs above the river to Jagat, a stone-paved village where the Manaslu Conservation Area checkpost checks your permits. The people of the lower gorge are mainly Gurung and Hindu hill families, growing millet, maize and rice. The heat in the gorge surprises many trekkers, so start early and carry water.

days.title: Philim and the turn into Tsum
days.text: Climb past Salleri and Sirdibas, where the first mani walls appear, to Philim, a large Gurung village. Beyond Ekle Bhatti the trail divides; you leave the Manaslu route for now and climb steeply through pine forest to Lokpa, the first village of Lower Tsum. You will come back to this junction in a week, heading up the main valley. From the ridge above Lokpa, the Shiar Khola gorge leads east into Tsum like a corridor.

days.title: Through the Shiar Khola gorge to Chumling
days.text: A quiet trail through pine and rhododendron above the Shiar Khola, with few houses and the sound of the river below. Chumling sits on a shelf above the gorge, with stone houses, potato and maize fields and an old gompa that the caretaker will usually open for a small offering. From here on, every village gate has a chorten and every wall has mani stones. Take the afternoon gently; the next days climb into the dry upper valley.

days.title: Up to Chhokangparo
days.text: Cross the river and climb through Rainjam and Gho into Upper Tsum, where the valley opens and forest gives way to barley fields. Chhokangparo is two villages side by side, Chhekam and Paro, on a broad terrace with Ganesh Himal to the south. Houses are close-built stone with flat roofs stacked with firewood. This is your first night above 3,000 m, the start of the acclimatisation that will carry you over the Larkya La in ten days.

days.title: Milarepa's cave and Nile
days.text: Walk through Lamagaon, with its long mani walls and chortens, to Piren Phu, a cave that tradition links with the yogi Milarepa, now a shrine with offerings and prayer flags. Continue past Burji and the bridge to Rachen Gompa to Nile, a stone village facing Chhule across the river. The upper valley is dry and open, with juniper, barley and yak pastures. Tibet is only a few days' walk north, along a route used by traders for centuries.

days.title: To Mu Gompa
days.text: A short climb up the open valley to Mu Gompa at 3,700 m, the largest monastery in Tsum, on a ridge near the head of the valley. The monks live here much of the year, and if a puja is under way, sit quietly at the back of the hall. In the afternoon, walk higher on the slope behind the monastery to help acclimatise, then come down to sleep. The night is cold and very still; this is as close to Tibet as the trek gets.

days.title: Down to Rachen Gompa
days.text: Descend the valley to Rachen Gompa, a large nunnery below the cliffs on the south side of the river. The nuns run their own kitchen, fields and school, and visitors can stay in the guesthouse when there is space. Ask your guide whether you may attend the evening prayers. After a week of steady climbing, this is a restful day, and the late light down the valley toward Ganesh Himal is among the trip's best moments.

days.title: Back down to Chumling
days.text: A long day down the valley, back through Chhokangparo, Gho and Rainjam to Chumling. The change from dry upper valley to green forest happens within a few hours. Your legs are now well used to the trail, and it is a good day to talk with your guide about the Nubri villages ahead, which share Tsum's faith but have their own dialect and customs. Tonight you sleep in Chumling again, in the same lodge as a week ago.

days.title: Out of Tsum and up to Deng
days.text: Walk back through the Shiar Khola gorge to Lokpa, drop to Ekle Bhatti and rejoin the main Budhi Gandaki trail, then climb north through bamboo forest above the river to Deng. This is where Nubri begins, and the people speak a Tibetan dialect related to, but distinct from, the one you heard in Tsum. Deng is small, a few lodges in a narrow valley, but after the climb out of Tsum it feels like a proper rest.

days.title: Ghap and Namrung
days.text: Cross the river and climb past Rana and Bihi Phedi through forest of fir and rhododendron, with langur monkeys in the trees. At Ghap, carved mani stones and chortens line the path; walk to the left of them, keeping them on your right, as local custom asks. The trail keeps climbing through forest to Namrung, where a checkpost looks at your Manaslu permit. Lodges here are good, and the dining rooms busy with trekkers heading to the pass.

days.title: Lihi, Sho and Lho
days.text: Above Namrung the forest opens into barley and buckwheat fields around Lihi and Sho, villages of stone and timber houses. Then Manaslu comes into view at the head of the valley, and it stays with you all the way to Samdo. Lho sits beneath it, with Ribung Gompa on the hill above. Walk up to the gompa in the late afternoon; sunset on Manaslu from here is one of the best mountain views in Nepal.

days.title: Shyala and Samagaon
days.text: A gentle climb through forest and meadow past Shyala, with Manaslu, Himal Chuli and Peak 29 in view, to Samagaon, the largest village in Nubri. Sama sits at the foot of the Manaslu glacier among yak pens and fields of barley and potato. After Tsum you will notice the altitude less than most trekkers here. Visit the village gompa in the afternoon and walk the lanes, where women work wool and children run between stone walls.

days.title: Pungyen Gompa or Birendra Tal
days.text: An acclimatisation day. Walk up to Pungyen Gompa beneath Manaslu's east face, a half-day outing to a monastery whose earlier building was destroyed by an avalanche in the 1950s, or climb part of the way toward Manaslu Base Camp for a bigger view of the glacier. In the afternoon, stroll to Birendra Tal, the glacial lake just below the village. Rest, eat well and keep drinking. The next four days take you over the pass.

days.title: Up the valley to Samdo
days.text: Follow the young Budhi Gandaki up a broad valley of juniper and yak pastures to Samdo, the highest permanent village on the route, near the old trade paths into Tibet. Because Tsum has already acclimatised you, we skip the usual second rest day here, but we keep the walk short and the afternoon free. Climb a little way up the ridge behind the village for an hour, then come down to sleep. Watch the yaks come home at dusk.

days.title: To Dharamsala below the pass
days.text: Cross the stream below Samdo and climb steadily past the ruins of Larkya Bazaar, an old seasonal trading post, to Dharamsala, also called Larkya Phedi. It is a cold, basic stop: a stone lodge, sometimes dormitory rooms or tents, and a crowded dining room in peak season. Eat early, pack for the morning and sleep by 7 pm. Anyone with serious altitude symptoms goes back down to Samdo rather than over the pass.

days.title: Larkya La and down to Bhimthang
days.text: Start around 4 am and climb by headtorch over moraine and false summits to the Larkya La at 5,106 m, hung with prayer flags. Himlung Himal, Cheo Himal, Kang Guru and Annapurna II spread out to the west. The descent is steep and can be icy near the top, so microspikes help late in the season. Lower down, the trail eases along moraine to Bhimthang, a meadow with lodges and pine trees. It is the longest and finest day of the three weeks.

days.title: Down through forest to Tilije
days.text: Cross the Dudh Khola and descend through rhododendron and pine past Karche and Gho to Tilije, a Gurung village of stone lanes and terraced fields. The thicker air and warmth after the pass feel wonderful, and your appetite will return in full. Fields of maize and buckwheat replace the yak pastures, and the houses change style again. Tonight is the last proper evening on the trail, so thank your porter and guide over a long dinner.

days.title: Dharapani and jeep to Besisahar
days.text: A short walk to Dharapani on the Marsyangdi, where your trail joins the Annapurna Circuit and the ACAP checkpost stamps your permit. A jeep takes you down the rough road through Tal, Chamje and Syange to Besisahar, the headquarters of Lamjung district. The road is narrow, with long drops to the river, but the drivers know every bend. A hot shower and a real mattress in Besisahar make a fine end to twenty nights on the trail.

days.title: Drive back to Kathmandu
days.text: A private car takes you down to Dumre on the Prithvi Highway and along the Trishuli river to Kathmandu, with lunch at a riverside stop. We drop you at your Kathmandu hotel in the afternoon, where the trip ends. If you would rather finish in Pokhara, the drive from Besisahar takes around four hours. Either way, keep at least one buffer night before an international flight in case of road delays.

good_to_know: Tsum and Manaslu are restricted areas: at least two trekkers, special permits and a licensed guide through a registered agency are required; check current status before you travel.
The Larkya La can be closed by snow, mostly from December to February; we suggest adding one spare day.
Upper Tsum keeps a local tradition against killing animals, so expect vegetarian meals there.
There are no ATMs after Arughat; carry enough Nepali rupees for three weeks.
Dharamsala below the pass is basic and very cold; bring a sleeping bag rated to about −15 °C.

faqs.q: Why do Tsum Valley before the Manaslu Circuit?
faqs.a: Because it acclimatises you. A week between 2,400 and 3,700 m in Tsum, including a night at Mu Gompa, prepares your body for Samagaon, Samdo and the Larkya La at 5,106 m. It also lets you see two Tibetan Buddhist valleys with different dialects and customs. Doing Tsum after the pass would mean retracing the whole gorge, which takes longer.

faqs.q: What permits do I need for the Manaslu and Tsum trek?
faqs.a: You need the Manaslu restricted area permit, the Tsum Valley restricted area permit, the Manaslu Conservation Area permit and, for the exit at Dharapani, the Annapurna Conservation Area permit. All are included and arranged through our agency. Groups must have at least two trekkers and a licensed guide. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How fit do I need to be for a 20-night trek?
faqs.a: Very fit and used to multi-day walking. You walk for 18 days, many of 6 to 7 hours, with an 8 to 10 hour pass day at 5,106 m. Training should include long hill walks on back-to-back days with a day pack for two to three months. Previous high-altitude trekking, such as Annapurna or Everest, is a real advantage.

faqs.q: Is the Manaslu and Tsum trek crowded?
faqs.a: No, not by Nepal standards. Tsum sees few trekkers even in October, and the Manaslu Circuit is far quieter than Everest or Annapurna. Samagaon and Dharamsala can be busy in peak weeks, and lodges at Dharamsala fill early. We book ahead where we can, and your guide manages the timing on pass day.

faqs.q: What is the best season for the Manaslu and Tsum Valley trek?
faqs.a: October and November give the most settled weather and the clearest views. April is the best spring month, with flowers in the forest and the pass usually open. March can still have heavy snow at Larkya La. December to February is cold and the pass is often closed, and the monsoon from June to August brings landslides and leeches.

faqs.q: Can a solo traveller do this trek?
faqs.a: Permits for Manaslu and Tsum are issued only to groups of at least two foreign trekkers with a licensed guide through a registered agency. If you are travelling alone, we can sometimes pair you with another trekker on the same dates for the permit, while you still walk at your own pace with your own guide. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Are there hot showers and wifi on the trek?
faqs.a: In many villages, yes, for a fee. Solar or gas hot showers are common in lodges along the Manaslu Circuit and in some Tsum villages. Wifi and mobile data are patchy; some lodges offer paid wifi, and phone coverage is available in parts of the lower valley and Samagaon. Monastery guest rooms in Tsum usually have neither.

faqs.q: What if the Larkya La is closed by snow?
faqs.a: We wait if there is time, which is why we suggest a spare day. If the pass stays closed, the safe option is to walk back down the Budhi Gandaki to Machha Khola and drive out, or in some cases fly by helicopter from Samagaon at extra cost. Your guide decides on the day, and safety always wins over the plan.

faqs.q: Do I need crampons or microspikes for the Larkya La?
faqs.a: Not usually in October, but microspikes are a good idea from mid-November and in spring, when the top of the pass and the steep descent can be icy. They are light and easy to fit. You do not need full crampons or technical gear. We can lend microspikes; tell us when you book.
